title: Μαχάων καὶ στίχες ἀνδρῶν
titleEn: The Healer and the Review of the Ranks — Iliad 4.183–271
part: The Healer and the Review of the Ranks (4.183–271)
about: Menelaus tells the army not to fear: belt, waistcloth and belly-guard stopped the arrow. Agamemnon sends the herald Talthybius to bring Machaon, son of the healer Asclepius, who is found among his troops from Tricca and comes through the army. Machaon draws out the arrow, undoes the armour, sucks out the blood and sprinkles on the gentle drugs that Chiron once gave his father. While they tend Menelaus the Trojan ranks advance and the Achaeans arm again. Agamemnon goes on foot along the ranks, cheering those who hasten and reviling those who hang back, and likens the idlers to fawns too tired to run. At the Cretans he praises Idomeneus for his place in war and at the feast; Idomeneus promises to stand by him and bids him rouse the others, since the Trojans broke the oaths and will pay.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἐπιθαρσύνων προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.l: Him, cheering on, addressed fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: Fair-haired Menelaus said to him, cheering him on:
sentences.n: A new speaker answers Agamemnon, whose speech ended the last part. τόν is the old pronoun use of the article, ‘him’, here Agamemnon. ἐπιθαρσύνων is the present participle of ἐπιθαρσύνω ‘cheer on, encourage’, built on θάρσος ‘courage’. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’, and ξανθός ‘fair-haired’ is the stock epithet of Menelaus, translated every time.

sentences.t: θάρσει, μηδέ τί πω δειδίσσεο λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l: “Take courage, and not at all yet frighten the people of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: “Take courage, and do not frighten the army of the Achaeans just yet;
sentences.n: θάρσει is the present imperative of θαρσέω ‘take courage’ (Attic θαρρέω), with -ρσ- where Attic has -ρρ-. μηδέ … δειδίσσεο is a prohibition: μή with the imperative, and δειδίσσεο is the present imperative middle (-εο for -ου) of δειδίσσομαι ‘frighten’, with λαόν ‘people, army’ as object. τί πω ‘at all yet’ softens it. Menelaus first quiets the army, before he speaks of the wound.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἐν καιρίῳ ὀξὺ πάγη βέλος, ἀλλὰ πάροιθεν
εἰρύσατο ζωστήρ τε παναίολος ἠδ’ ὑπένερθε
ζῶμά τε καὶ μίτρη, τὴν χαλκῆες κάμον ἄνδρες.
sentences.l:
not in a vital place was the sharp shaft fixed, but in front
guarded (me) the belt, the all-glancing, and underneath
the waistcloth and the belly-guard, which bronzesmiths toiled to make, men.”
sentences.i: The sharp shaft was not fixed in a vital place, but my all-glancing belt guarded me in front, and underneath it the waistcloth and the belly-guard, which men, smiths of bronze, toiled to make.”
sentences.n: The reason for ‘take courage’, in one sentence whose verb εἰρύσατο waits until the second line. ἐν καιρίῳ is ‘in a vital place’ (an adjective with a noun understood), πάγη the aorist passive of πήγνυμι ‘fix’, and ὀξὺ βέλος ‘sharp shaft’ the subject. εἰρύσατο ‘guarded’ (aorist middle of ἐρύομαι, with lengthened εἰ-) has three subjects: ζωστήρ ‘belt’, ζῶμα ‘waistcloth’, μίτρη ‘belly-guard’, in the order πάροιθεν ‘in front’, ὑπένερθε ‘underneath’. παναίολος is παν- ‘all’ + αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’; whether the belt gleams or is many-coloured is not certain. κάμον is an unaugmented aorist of κάμνω ‘toil’, and ἄνδρες stands beside χαλκῆες ‘bronzesmiths’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed lord Agamemnon:
sentences.i: In answer lord Agamemnon said to him:
sentences.n: The reply formula, as at 1.130: τόν ‘him’ is Menelaus, ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is the middle participle of ἀπαμείβομαι, and προσέφη ‘addressed’ is as at 183. κρείων ‘lord’ is the stock word of rank for Agamemnon here; it is not the same word as ἄναξ in ‘lord of men’, and the two are told apart by context. A new paragraph begins at 188.

sentences.t: αἲ γὰρ δὴ οὕτως εἴη φίλος ὦ Μενέλαε·
sentences.l: “Would that it were so indeed, dear Menelaus;
sentences.i: “If only it were so indeed, dear Menelaus;
sentences.n: αἲ γὰρ … εἴη is a wish: αἲ γάρ ‘would that’ with the optative εἴη ‘may it be’ (a wish that can be fulfilled). οὕτως ‘so’ points back to what Menelaus has just said: that the wound is not mortal. δή adds ‘indeed’. φίλος ὦ Μενέλαε is a vocative, ‘dear Menelaus’, with ὦ placed between the adjective and the name.

sentences.t:
ἕλκος δ’ ἰητὴρ ἐπιμάσσεται ἠδ’ ἐπιθήσει
φάρμαχ’ ἅ κεν παύσῃσι μελαινάων ὀδυνάων.
sentences.l:
the wound a healer will touch, and will lay on
drugs which may make (it) cease from black pains.”
sentences.i: A healer will touch the wound and lay on drugs that will stop the black pains.”
sentences.n: ἕλκος ‘wound’ is the object of both verbs, ἐπιμάσσεται ‘will touch’ (future of ἐπιμάσσομαι) and ἐπιθήσει ‘will lay on’ (future of ἐπιτίθημι); ἰητήρ ‘healer’ is the subject. φάρμαχ’ is φάρμακα ‘drugs’, elided, and ἅ κεν παύσῃσι is a relative clause with κε and a subjunctive in -σι (3 pl.). παύω takes a genitive of what is ended, so ‘make cease from black pains’, the thing that ceases being left unsaid. μελαινάων ὀδυνάων is the epic genitive plural (-άων = -ῶν).

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ Ταλθύβιον θεῖον κήρυκα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: He spoke, and he addressed Talthybius, the divine herald:
sentences.i: So he said, and spoke to Talthybius, the divine herald:
sentences.n: ἦ καί is ‘he spoke, and’, the old way of closing one speech and starting the action that follows; here the action is a second speech. Ταλθύβιον is the accusative object of προσηύδα (imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’), with θεῖον κήρυκα ‘the divine herald’ beside it; θεῖος ‘divine’ is a word of honour for the herald. A new paragraph begins at 192.

sentences.t:
Ταλθύβι’ ὅττι τάχιστα Μαχάονα δεῦρο κάλεσσον
φῶτ’ Ἀσκληπιοῦ υἱὸν ἀμύμονος ἰητῆρος,
sentences.l:
“Talthybius, as quickly as possible Machaon here summon,
the man, the son of Asclepius, the blameless healer,
sentences.i: “Talthybius, summon Machaon here as quickly as you can, the man, son of Asclepius the blameless healer,
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s order, to be cut at the comma because the whole sentence runs to five lines. Ταλθύβι’ is the elided vocative of Ταλθύβιος; ὅττι τάχιστα (ὅττι = ὅ τι) is ‘as quickly as possible’; κάλεσσον is the aorist imperative of καλέω ‘summon’, with doubled σ. φῶτ’ ‘man’ is in apposition to Μαχάονα. Ἀσκληπιοῦ υἱόν is ‘son of Asclepius’, and ἀμύμονος ἰητῆρος, in the genitive, belongs to Asclepius: ‘the blameless healer’. ἀμύμων is a stock epithet whose real sense is not known.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα ἴδῃ Μενέλαον ἀρήϊον Ἀτρέος υἱόν,
ὅν τις ὀϊστεύσας ἔβαλεν τόξων ἐῢ εἰδὼς
Τρώων ἢ Λυκίων, τῷ μὲν κλέος, ἄμμι δὲ πένθος.
sentences.l:
so that he may see Menelaus, the warlike son of Atreus,
whom someone, having shot an arrow, struck, well knowing the bow,
of the Trojans or of the Lycians, to him glory, but to us grief.”
sentences.i: so that he may see Menelaus, the warlike son of Atreus, whom someone who knew the bow well has hit with an arrow, a Trojan or a Lycian: glory for him, but grief for us.”
sentences.n: ὄφρα ἴδῃ ‘so that he may see’ is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive. Menelaus is the object, with ἀρήϊον ‘warlike’ and Ἀτρέος υἱόν ‘son of Atreus’. In ὅν … ἔβαλεν ‘whom … struck’ the subject is τις ‘someone’, with ὀϊστεύσας ‘having shot an arrow’ and τόξων ἐῢ εἰδώς ‘knowing the bow well’; Τρώων ἢ Λυκίων says only which side. τῷ μὲν … ἄμμι δέ sets ‘for him’ against ‘for us’ (ἄμμι is the Aeolic form of ἡμῖν): glory against grief. Lines 206–207 repeat 196–197 word for word.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἄρα οἱ κῆρυξ ἀπίθησεν ἀκούσας,
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι κατὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
παπταίνων ἥρωα Μαχάονα·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the herald did not disobey him when he heard, but set out through the army of the bronze-shirted Achaeans, looking about for the hero Machaon;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech. οἱ is the old pronoun in the dative, ‘him’, and ἀπίθησεν the aorist of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’; ἀκούσας ‘having heard’ gives the ground of obedience. βῆ δ’ ἰέναι ‘set out to go’ is a stock phrase, βῆ being the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω. κατά with the accusative λαόν ‘people, army’ means ‘through’. χαλκοχιτώνων ‘bronze-shirted’ is the stock epithet of the Achaeans, translated every time. The unit ends in the middle of line 200.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ νόησεν
ἑσταότ’·
sentences.l:
and him he noticed
standing;
sentences.i: and he noticed him standing there;
sentences.n: τὸν δὲ νόησεν is the second half of line 200: τόν is the pronoun ‘him’, Machaon, and νόησεν the unaugmented aorist of νοέω ‘notice, perceive’. ἑσταότ’ is ἑσταότα, elided: the perfect participle of ἵστημι in its epic form (Attic ἑστῶτα), ‘standing’, agreeing with τόν. This short unit starts and ends in the middle of a line, because the colon falls inside lines 200 and 201.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ μιν κρατεραὶ στίχες ἀσπιστάων
λαῶν, οἵ οἱ ἕποντο Τρίκης ἐξ ἱπποβότοιο.
sentences.l:
and about him the strong ranks of shield-bearing
people, who followed him from horse-pasturing Tricca.
sentences.i: and around him were the strong ranks of his shield-bearing troops, who had followed him from horse-pasturing Tricca.
sentences.n: This unit starts in the middle of line 201. ἀμφὶ δέ μιν ‘and about him’ takes μιν, the epic pronoun, ‘him’ (Machaon). στίχες ‘ranks’ is the subject, with ἀσπιστάων ‘shield-bearing’ (epic genitive plural in -άων) and λαῶν ‘of troops’. οἵ οἱ ἕποντο: the first οἵ is the relative ‘who’, the second οἱ is ‘him’, and ἕποντο is the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. Tricca is the Thessalian town that the Catalogue gave to Machaon’s troops (2.729–732); ἱππόβοτος ‘horse-pasturing’ is its epithet.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: and standing close by, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and, standing close beside him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ ‘close by’ and ἱστάμενος ‘standing’ (present participle middle of ἵστημι) give the speaker’s place, beside the man he addresses. ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the formula for words that fly from speaker to hearer; ἔπεα is the uncontracted plural of ἔπος. προσηύδα ‘spoke to’ is the imperfect of προσαυδάω. The whole line stands, with the same English, in the Odyssey (and with ‘she’ at 4.92).

sentences.t:
ὄρσ’ Ἀσκληπιάδη, καλέει κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων,
ὄφρα ἴδῃς Μενέλαον ἀρήϊον ἀρχὸν Ἀχαιῶν,
ὅν τις ὀϊστεύσας ἔβαλεν τόξων ἐῢ εἰδὼς
Τρώων ἢ Λυκίων, τῷ μὲν κλέος, ἄμμι δὲ πένθος.
sentences.l:
“Rise up, Asclepius’-son, he summons you, lord Agamemnon,
so that you may see Menelaus, the warlike leader of the Achaeans,
whom someone, having shot an arrow, struck, well knowing the bow,
of the Trojans or of the Lycians, to him glory, but to us grief.”
sentences.i: “Rise up, son of Asclepius: lord Agamemnon is calling you, so that you may see Menelaus, the warlike commander of the Achaeans, whom someone who knew the bow well has hit with an arrow, a Trojan or a Lycian: glory for him, but grief for us.”
sentences.n: The herald delivers the order. ὄρσ’ is ὄρσο, the aorist imperative middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, so ‘rise up’; Ἀσκληπιάδη is the vocative of the patronymic Ἀσκληπιάδης ‘son of Asclepius’; καλέει is the uncontracted epic present of καλέω ‘call’, and κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων ‘lord Agamemnon’ is the subject. Lines 206–207 repeat 196–197 exactly, and line 205 differs from 195 only in ἴδῃς ‘you may see’ for ἴδῃ, and ἀρχὸν Ἀχαιῶν ‘leader of the Achaeans’ for Ἀτρέος υἱόν.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῷ δ’ ἄρα θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ὄρινε·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and in him the heart in his breast he stirred.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and he stirred the heart in Machaon’s breast.
sentences.n: A closing formula with its effect: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ (φάτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of φημί), and τῷ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and in him’, the old pronoun in the dative, standing for Machaon, not for the herald who has spoken. θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ὄρινε is ‘stirred the heart in the breast’ (ὄρινε the unaugmented aorist of ὀρίνω; στήθεσσιν the epic dative plural). The English names Machaon, because ‘his breast’ alone would seem to be the speaker’s. A new paragraph begins at 208.

sentences.t: βὰν δ’ ἰέναι καθ’ ὅμιλον ἀνὰ στρατὸν εὐρὺν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: And they set out to go down through the throng, up through the wide army of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: And they set out to go through the throng, up and down the wide army of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: βὰν δ’ ἰέναι ‘and they set out to go’: βάν is the unaugmented 3 pl. aorist of βαίνω (= ἔβησαν), here the herald and Machaon together, and ἰέναι is the infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’; the phrase is the plural of the βῆ δ’ ἰέναι of 199. κατά with ὅμιλον ‘throng’ and ἀνά with στρατόν ‘army’ are an old pair, ‘down … up’, meaning to and fro. εὐρὺν Ἀχαιῶν ‘wide’ describes the army, as at 1.478.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἵκανον ὅθι ξανθὸς Μενέλαος
βλήμενος ἦν, περὶ δ’ αὐτὸν ἀγηγέραθ’ ὅσσοι ἄριστοι
κυκλόσ’, ὃ δ’ ἐν μέσσοισι παρίστατο ἰσόθεος φώς,
αὐτίκα δ’ ἐκ ζωστῆρος ἀρηρότος ἕλκεν ὀϊστόν·
sentences.l:
But when indeed they came to where fair-haired Menelaus
lay struck, and around him were gathered all the best men
in a ring, and he in the midst stood beside, a man equal to a god,
and at once from the fitted belt he drew the arrow;
sentences.i: But when they came to the place where fair-haired Menelaus lay struck, with all the best men gathered around him in a ring, Machaon, a man the equal of a god, stood beside him in the midst of them, and at once he drew the arrow out of the close-fitting belt;
sentences.n: One sentence of four lines, with the main verb ἕλκεν in the last. ἵκανον is the unaugmented aorist of ἱκάνω ‘come to’; ἦν βλήμενος ‘lay struck’ pairs ἦν with an aorist participle middle of βάλλω. ἀγηγέραθ’ is ἀγηγέρατο, ‘were gathered’, and κυκλόσ’ is κυκλόσε ‘in a ring’. At ὃ δ’ the subject changes: ὅ is Machaon, ‘he’, and ἰσόθεος φώς ‘a man the equal of a god’ is a stock phrase applied to him. ἀρηρότος is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, so ‘the fitted belt’; ἕλκεν is an imperfect, ‘was drawing’.

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ ἐξελκομένοιο πάλιν ἄγεν ὀξέες ὄγκοι.
sentences.l: and as it was drawn out, back were bent the sharp barbs.
sentences.i: and as it was drawn out, the sharp barbs were bent back.
sentences.n: τοῦ δ’ ἐξελκομένοιο is a genitive absolute, ‘as it was being drawn out’: τοῦ is ‘it’, the arrow, and ἐξελκομένοιο is a present passive participle in the epic genitive -οιο. ὀξέες ὄγκοι ‘the sharp barbs’ is the subject; ὄγκος means ‘barb’ on the usual explanation. ἄγεν is read as a 3 pl. aorist passive of ἄγνυμι ‘break’ (= ἐάγησαν), ‘were bent back’; the form is not certain, and the sense given is the usual one.

sentences.t:
λῦσε δέ οἱ ζωστῆρα παναίολον ἠδ’ ὑπένερθε
ζῶμά τε καὶ μίτρην, τὴν χαλκῆες κάμον ἄνδρες.
sentences.l:
And he loosed for him the belt, the all-glancing, and underneath
the waistcloth and the belly-guard, which bronzesmiths toiled to make, men.
sentences.i: He undid the all-glancing belt for him, and underneath it the waistcloth and the belly-guard, which men, smiths of bronze, toiled to make.
sentences.n: Machaon takes off the three pieces that stopped the arrow, in the order Menelaus named them (185–187): the belt, then underneath it the waistcloth and the belly-guard. λῦσε is the unaugmented aorist of λύω, and οἱ ‘for him’ a dative of interest. The second line is 187 again, with μίτρην (accusative) for μίτρη. ζῶμα, a girdle or loin-cloth, is a different word from ζωστήρ ‘belt’; the belly-guard (μίτρη) is a guard of metal.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ἴδεν ἕλκος ὅθ’ ἔμπεσε πικρὸς ὀϊστός,
αἷμ’ ἐκμυζήσας ἐπ’ ἄρ’ ἤπια φάρμακα εἰδὼς
πάσσε, τά οἵ ποτε πατρὶ φίλα φρονέων πόρε Χείρων.
sentences.l:
But when he saw the wound where the bitter arrow had fallen in,
the blood having sucked out, then on it gentle drugs, knowing them,
he sprinkled, which to his father once, thinking kindly, Chiron gave.
sentences.i: But when he saw the wound where the bitter arrow had fallen in, he sucked out the blood and sprinkled on it the gentle drugs that he knew, which Chiron, kindly disposed, had once given to his father.
sentences.n: ἴδεν and ἔμπεσε are unaugmented aorists, ‘saw’ and ‘fell in’; ὅθ’ is ὅθι ‘where’. ἐκμυζήσας is an aorist participle of ἐκμυζάω ‘suck out’. ἐπ’ … πάσσε is tmesis: ἐπιπάσσω ‘sprinkle on’ with its preposition set apart. εἰδώς, the perfect participle of οἶδα, takes ἤπια φάρμακα ‘gentle drugs’ as object, ‘knowing them’, as a skilled man does. τά οἵ ποτε πατρὶ πόρε: τά ‘which’ is the old demonstrative used as a relative, οἵ ‘to him’ and πατρί ‘to his father’ together mean ‘to his father’; φίλα φρονέων is ‘thinking kindly’. Chiron is named with no introduction, as a figure of tradition.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα τοὶ ἀμφεπένοντο βοὴν ἀγαθὸν Μενέλαον,
τόφρα δ’ ἐπὶ Τρώων στίχες ἤλυθον ἀσπιστάων·
sentences.l:
While they were busying themselves about Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
meanwhile came on the ranks of the shield-bearing Trojans;
sentences.i: While they were busying themselves about Menelaus, good at the war-cry, the ranks of the shield-bearing Trojans came on;
sentences.n: ὄφρα … τόφρα ‘while … meanwhile’ sets two actions side by side. τοί is the old pronoun, ‘they’, the Achaeans; ἀμφεπένοντο is the imperfect of ἀμφιπένομαι ‘busy oneself about’, with Μενέλαον in the accusative, and βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is his stock epithet. ἐπὶ … ἤλυθον is tmesis, ἐπῆλθον ‘advanced against’ (ἤλυθον = ἦλθον). ἀσπιστάων ‘shield-bearing’ agrees with Τρώων. A new paragraph begins at 220.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ αὖτις κατὰ τεύχε’ ἔδυν, μνήσαντο δὲ χάρμης.
sentences.l: and they again into their armour entered, and remembered the joy of battle.
sentences.i: and the Achaeans put on their armour again and remembered the joy of battle.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ can only be the Achaeans, who had put off their arms during the truce and now arm again: that is why the English names them. κατὰ τεύχε’ ἔδυν is tmesis, ‘went down into their armour’, i.e. put it on (τεύχε’ is τεύχεα, elided; ἔδυν is a 3 pl. aorist of δύω). μνήσαντο is the aorist middle of μιμνήσκομαι ‘remember’, with the genitive χάρμης ‘joy in fighting’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ οὐκ ἂν βρίζοντα ἴδοις Ἀγαμέμνονα δῖον
οὐδὲ καταπτώσσοντ’ οὐδ’ οὐκ ἐθέλοντα μάχεσθαι,
ἀλλὰ μάλα σπεύδοντα μάχην ἐς κυδιάνειραν.
sentences.l:
Then you would not have seen heavenly Agamemnon drowsing,
nor cowering, nor unwilling to fight,
but hastening greatly to the man-glorifying battle.
sentences.i: Then you would not have seen heavenly Agamemnon drowsing, nor cowering, nor unwilling to fight, but hastening eagerly to the battle that brings men glory.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ οὐκ ἂν ἴδοις is a potential optative with ‘you’ meaning anyone who might have watched: ‘you would not have seen’. Three accusative participles agree with Ἀγαμέμνονα δῖον: βρίζοντα ‘drowsing’ (βρίζω ‘nod with sleep’), καταπτώσσοντ’ ‘cowering’, and οὐκ ἐθέλοντα ‘unwilling’, after οὐδ’ … οὐδ’; then ἀλλὰ μάλα σπεύδοντα ‘but hastening greatly’. κυδιάνειραν is κῦδος ‘glory’ + ἀνήρ ‘man’. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is a stock epithet, translated every time. A new paragraph begins at 223.

sentences.t: ἵππους μὲν γὰρ ἔασε καὶ ἅρματα ποικίλα χαλκῷ·
sentences.l: for his horses he had left, and his chariot, intricate with bronze;
sentences.i: For he had left his horses and his chariot, intricately worked with bronze;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason why Agamemnon is on foot (231). ἔασε is the aorist of ἐάω ‘let be, leave’. ἵππους ‘horses’ and ἅρματα ‘chariot’ are the objects; the plural ἅρματα is common for one chariot. ποικίλα χαλκῷ is ‘intricate with bronze’: ποικίλος means worked in a pattern, and the dative χαλκῷ says what the pattern is made of.

sentences.t:
καὶ τοὺς μὲν θεράπων ἀπάνευθ’ ἔχε φυσιόωντας
Εὐρυμέδων υἱὸς Πτολεμαίου Πειραΐδαο·
sentences.l:
and them, apart, his attendant kept, snorting,
Eurymedon, son of Ptolemaeus, Peiraeus’-son;
sentences.i: and his attendant Eurymedon, son of Ptolemaeus, son of Peiraeus, held them to one side, snorting;
sentences.n: καὶ τοὺς μέν ‘and them’ (the horses) has a μέν that waits for αὐτὰρ ὃ ‘but he himself’ in 231. θεράπων ‘attendant’ is the subject, named in the next line as Εὐρυμέδων, with the patronymic Πτολεμαίου Πειραΐδαο: Ptolemaeus, son of Peiraeus (the epic genitive -αο). ἀπάνευθ’ is ἀπάνευθε ‘apart’, ἔχε the imperfect ‘was holding’, and φυσιόωντας the uncontracted participle (Attic φυσιῶντας) of φυσιάω ‘blow, snort’.

sentences.t:
τῷ μάλα πόλλ’ ἐπέτελλε παρισχέμεν ὁππότε κέν μιν
γυῖα λάβῃ κάματος πολέας διὰ κοιρανέοντα·
sentences.l:
to him very many commands he gave, to hold them ready, whenever him
in the limbs weariness should seize, through the many acting as ruler;
sentences.i: he had charged him strictly to hold them ready, whenever weariness should seize his limbs as he went through the many, acting as their ruler;
sentences.n: τῷ ‘to him’ is Eurymedon; ἐπέτελλε is the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω ‘lay a charge on’, and μάλα πόλλ’ ‘very many things’ makes it strict. παρισχέμεν is the epic infinitive of παρέχω ‘hold ready’, the horses being understood. ὁππότε κέν … λάβῃ is a general clause, κέν with an aorist subjunctive: μιν ‘him’ (Agamemnon) is the object, γυῖα ‘in the limbs’ the part affected, κάματος ‘weariness’ the subject. πολέας διὰ κοιρανέοντα is ‘through the many, acting as ruler’, κοιρανέοντα agreeing with μιν.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ πεζὸς ἐὼν ἐπεπωλεῖτο στίχας ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l: but he himself, being on foot, was going about the ranks of men;
sentences.i: but he himself, on foot, ranged along the ranks of men;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ ‘but he’, with ὅ the old pronoun, is Agamemnon, and πεζὸς ἐών ‘being on foot’ gives the consequence of 226 (ἐών is the epic participle of εἰμί, Attic ὤν). ἐπεπωλεῖτο is the imperfect of ἐπιπωλέομαι ‘go over, range along’: the imperfect shows that the going to and fro is kept up. στίχας ἀνδρῶν ‘ranks of men’ is the object. Line 250 will repeat this half-line.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ οὓς μὲν σπεύδοντας ἴδοι Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων,
τοὺς μάλα θαρσύνεσκε παριστάμενος ἐπέεσσιν·
sentences.l:
and whichever of the swift-colted Danaans he saw hastening,
them greatly he would cheer, standing beside them, with words;
sentences.i: And whichever of the Danaans with their swift colts he saw hastening, those he would heartily cheer with his words, standing beside them;
sentences.n: Two verbs show what happened again and again: ἴδοι (optative) and θαρσύνεσκε, an imperfect with the iterative -σκε, together mean ‘whenever he saw …, he would cheer’. καί ῥ’ is καὶ ἄρα. οὓς μέν … τοὺς … ‘whichever … them’; the μέν looks ahead to the other group in 240. ταχυπώλων is ταχύς ‘swift’ + πῶλος ‘colt’, a stock epithet of the Danaans, translated every time. σπεύδοντας ‘hastening’ and παριστάμενος ‘standing beside’ are participles; ἐπέεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ἔπος.

sentences.t: Ἀργεῖοι μή πώ τι μεθίετε θούριδος ἀλκῆς·
sentences.l: “Argives, do not at all yet slacken from impetuous might;
sentences.i: “Argives, do not slacken yet in your impetuous might;
sentences.n: Ἀργεῖοι ‘Argives’ is one of the army’s three names, and the poet’s choice is kept in English. μή with the present imperative μεθίετε is a prohibition: μεθίημι ‘let go, slacken’, with the genitive of what is let go. μή πώ τι is ‘not yet at all’. θούριδος ἀλκῆς is ‘impetuous might’: ἀλκή is strength in fighting, and θοῦρις is a feminine adjective ‘rushing, impetuous’ (cf. θοῦρος).

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ ψευδέσσι πατὴρ Ζεὺς ἔσσετ’ ἀρωγός,
ἀλλ’ οἵ περ πρότεροι ὑπὲρ ὅρκια δηλήσαντο
τῶν ἤτοι αὐτῶν τέρενα χρόα γῦπες ἔδονται,
sentences.i: for father Zeus will not be a helper of liars; but as for those who were the first to do harm in breach of the oaths, the vultures will eat the tender skin of those very men,
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason: Zeus helps no one who lies. ἔσσετ’ is ἔσσεται ‘will be’, ἀρωγός ‘helper’ (cf. ἀρήγω ‘help’), and ἐπὶ ψευδέσσι ‘on the side of liars’ is ἐπί with the dative of ψευδής. Then comes the turn: οἵ περ πρότεροι ὑπὲρ ὅρκια δηλήσαντο ‘those who first did harm beyond the oaths’ (δηλήσαντο, aorist middle of δηλέομαι), the same clause as in 4.67 and 4.72. τῶν … αὐτῶν ‘of those very men’ goes with χρόα ‘skin’; τέρενα is the neuter plural of τέρην ‘tender’; ἔδονται is the epic future of ἔδω ‘eat’. The sentence waits for ἡμεῖς in the next line; it is cut at this comma because it would run to five lines.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς αὖτ’ ἀλόχους τε φίλας καὶ νήπια τέκνα
ἄξομεν ἐν νήεσσιν, ἐπὴν πτολίεθρον ἕλωμεν.
sentences.l:
we, in turn, dear wives and infant children
will bring in our ships, when we have taken the citadel.”
sentences.i: while we, for our part, will bring their dear wives and little children away in our ships, when we have taken the citadel.”
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς αὖτ’ ‘we, in turn’ answers the vultures of 237: the oath-breakers’ end set against the Achaeans’ gain. ἀλόχους … φίλας ‘dear wives’ and νήπια τέκνα ‘infant children’ are the objects of ἄξομεν ‘we shall bring’ (future of ἄγω); the Greek has no ‘their’, but the wives are the Trojans’. ἐν νήεσσιν ‘in ships’ has the epic dative plural of ναῦς. ἐπὴν … ἕλωμεν ‘when we have taken’ is ἐπεὶ ἄν with the aorist subjunctive of αἱρέω, and πτολίεθρον ‘citadel’ is Troy.

sentences.t:
οὕς τινας αὖ μεθιέντας ἴδοι στυγεροῦ πολέμοιο,
τοὺς μάλα νεικείεσκε χολωτοῖσιν ἐπέεσσιν·
sentences.l:
And whichever in turn he saw slackening from hateful war,
them greatly he would revile with angry words:
sentences.i: But whichever of them he saw slackening from hateful war, those he would revile sharply with angry words:
sentences.n: The second half of the pair begun at 232: οὕς τινας αὖ … ἴδοι ‘and whichever, in turn, he saw’ and νεικείεσκε, the iterative imperfect of νεικείω ‘revile’, again mean ‘whenever … he would’. μεθιέντας is the present participle of μεθίημι ‘slacken’, with the genitive στυγεροῦ πολέμοιο ‘from hateful war’, as μεθίετε took ἀλκῆς in 234. χολωτοῖσιν ἐπέεσσιν ‘with angry words’: χολωτός is from χόλος ‘anger’. A new paragraph begins at 240.

sentences.t: Ἀργεῖοι ἰόμωροι ἐλεγχέες οὔ νυ σέβεσθε;
sentences.l: “Argives, arrow-dull, shameful ones, do you not then feel shame?
sentences.i: “Argives, you dull archers, you shameful ones, have you no shame?
sentences.n: Three vocatives open the speech: Ἀργεῖοι, ἰόμωροι, ἐλεγχέες. ἰόμωροι occurs only here and its meaning is not known; one guess builds it from ἰός ‘arrow’ and μῶρος ‘dull’, and the English gives that guess. ἐλεγχέες is the plural of ἐλεγχής ‘shameful, disgraceful’. οὔ νυ σέβεσθε; ‘do you not then feel shame?’ is a question (the edition prints ;); σέβομαι ‘feel awe, feel shame’ is used without an object. A new paragraph begins at 242.

sentences.t:
τίφθ’ οὕτως ἔστητε τεθηπότες ἠΰτε νεβροί,
αἵ τ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν ἔκαμον πολέος πεδίοιο θέουσαι
ἑστᾶσ’, οὐδ’ ἄρα τίς σφι μετὰ φρεσὶ γίγνεται ἀλκή·
sentences.i: Why do you stand there so stunned, like fawns that, when they have tired of running over a great plain, stand still, with no might at all arising in their wits;
sentences.n: τίφθ’ is τίπτε ‘why’ elided before a rough breathing (π + h = φ). ἔστητε is the aorist of ἵστημι in its intransitive sense, ‘you stand’, and τεθηπότες the perfect participle of a verb whose perfect τέθηπα means ‘be astonished, stunned’. The simile is a general truth: αἵ τ’ ‘which (as they do)’, ἔκαμον an aorist of κάμνω used for what always happens, ‘have tired’, πολέος πεδίοιο a genitive of the ground crossed, ἑστᾶσ’ the 3 pl. perfect ἑστᾶσι ‘stand’, σφι ‘to them’. νεβροί ‘fawns’ and ἀλκή ‘might’ (cf. 234).

sentences.t: ὣς ὑμεῖς ἔστητε τεθηπότες οὐδὲ μάχεσθε.
sentences.l: so you stand stunned, nor do you fight.
sentences.i: So you stand there stunned and do not fight.
sentences.n: ὣς ὑμεῖς ‘so you’ closes the simile and turns it on the hearers. ἔστητε τεθηπότες repeats the words of 243, and οὐδὲ μάχεσθε ‘and you do not fight’ says what the standing amounts to. The fawns have lost their strength by running; the Argives, he implies, have not even run.

sentences.l:
Or are you waiting for the Trojans to come near, where the ships
are drawn up, the well-sterned ones, on the shore of the grey sea,
so that you may see whether over you the son of Cronus will hold his hand?”
sentences.i: Or are you waiting for the Trojans to come near, to where the well-sterned ships are drawn up on the shore of the grey sea, so that you may see whether the son of Cronus will hold his hand over you?”
sentences.n: ἦ … ; opens a sharp question, ‘or are you waiting …?’. μένετε takes Τρῶας σχεδὸν ἐλθέμεν ‘the Trojans to come near’, ἐλθέμεν being the epic infinitive of ἔρχομαι. εἰρύατ’ is εἰρύαται, the 3 pl. perfect passive of ἐρύω ‘draw’, so ‘are drawn up’ on the beach; εὔπρυμνοι is εὖ + πρύμνη ‘stern’, ‘well-sterned’, a stock word for ships. πολιῆς … θαλάσσης is the ‘grey sea’. ὔμμιν is the Aeolic ὑμῖν ‘to you’, and ὑπέρσχῃ χεῖρα ‘hold his hand over’ is the picture of a protector; Κρονίων ‘the son of Cronus’ is Zeus, who has just been said to help no liars.

sentences.t: ὣς ὅ γε κοιρανέων ἐπεπωλεῖτο στίχας ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l: Thus he, acting as ruler, went about the ranks of men;
sentences.i: So he ranged along the ranks of men as their ruler;
sentences.n: ὣς ὅ γε ‘so he’ closes the scene begun at 231, and κοιρανέων ‘acting as ruler’ and ἐπεπωλεῖτο στίχας ἀνδρῶν repeat the words of 230–231. The paragraph that begins here carries Agamemnon from the Danaans in general to the Cretans.

sentences.t: ἦλθε δ’ ἐπὶ Κρήτεσσι κιὼν ἀνὰ οὐλαμὸν ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.l: and he came upon the Cretans, going up through the crowd of men.
sentences.i: And, making his way through the crowd of men, he came upon the Cretans.
sentences.n: ἦλθε δ’ ἐπὶ Κρήτεσσι is ‘and he came upon the Cretans’: ἐπί with the dative after a verb of coming gives ‘up to, upon’, and Κρήτεσσι is the epic dative plural of Κρής. κιών is the participle of κίω ‘go’. ἀνὰ οὐλαμὸν ἀνδρῶν ‘up through the crowd of men’ uses the rare word οὐλαμός ‘crowd, press’.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἀμφ’ Ἰδομενῆα δαΐφρονα θωρήσσοντο·
sentences.l: and they about Idomeneus, the wise-minded, were arming themselves;
sentences.i: and they were arming themselves around wise-hearted Idomeneus;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the Cretans. ἀμφ’ Ἰδομενῆα is ἀμφί with the accusative, ‘about Idomeneus’ (epic accusative in -ῆα), and θωρήσσοντο is the imperfect middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, built on θώρηξ ‘breastplate’. δαΐφρων is a stock epithet whose sense is disputed: ‘wise-minded’ (from δαῆναι ‘learn’) or ‘fierce-minded’ (from δάϊος ‘hostile’). The English takes the first.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεὺς μὲν ἐνὶ προμάχοις συῒ εἴκελος ἀλκήν,
Μηριόνης δ’ ἄρα οἱ πυμάτας ὄτρυνε φάλαγγας.
sentences.l:
Idomeneus among the foremost fighters, like a boar in might,
and Meriones, then, for him the rearmost battle-lines urged on.
sentences.i: Idomeneus, among the foremost fighters, was like a boar in might, and Meriones was urging on the rearmost battle-lines for him.
sentences.n: μέν … δέ pairs the two leaders, one in front and one behind. ἐνὶ προμάχοις is ‘among the foremost fighters’ (πρόμαχος ‘fighter in the front’), συῒ εἴκελος ‘like a boar’ (the diaeresis shows that συῒ is two syllables), and ἀλκήν is an accusative of respect, ‘in might’. πυμάτας ‘rearmost’ goes with φάλαγγας ‘battle-lines’, the object of ὄτρυνε, an unaugmented imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’; οἱ is ‘for him’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δὲ ἰδὼν γήθησεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων,
αὐτίκα δ’ Ἰδομενῆα προσηύδα μειλιχίοισιν·
sentences.l:
And seeing them, he rejoiced, the lord of men, Agamemnon,
and at once to Idomeneus he spoke with gentle ones:
sentences.i: Seeing them, Agamemnon, lord of men, rejoiced, and at once spoke to Idomeneus with gentle words:
sentences.n: τοὺς δὲ ἰδών ‘and seeing them’: τούς is the pronoun ‘them’, the Cretans, and ἰδών the aorist participle of ὁράω. γήθησεν is the aorist of γηθέω ‘rejoice’. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is the stock epithet of Agamemnon, translated every time. μειλιχίοισιν ‘with gentle ones’ is an adjective in the dative plural standing alone for μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσιν ‘with gentle words’, the noun being understood.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεῦ περὶ μέν σε τίω Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων
ἠμὲν ἐνὶ πτολέμῳ ἠδ’ ἀλλοίῳ ἐπὶ ἔργῳ
ἠδ’ ἐν δαίθ’, ὅτε πέρ τε γερούσιον αἴθοπα οἶνον
Ἀργείων οἳ ἄριστοι ἐνὶ κρητῆρι κέρωνται.
sentences.l:
“Idomeneus, above the Danaans of the swift colts I honour you,
both in war and in any other work,
and at the feast, when the elders’ fire-faced wine
the best of the Argives mix in the mixing-bowl.
sentences.i: “Idomeneus, I honour you above the Danaans with their swift colts, both in war and in any other work, and at the feast, whenever the best of the Argives mix the elders’ wine, that has the look of fire, in the mixing-bowl.
sentences.n: The main verb is τίω ‘I honour’, with σε ‘you’; περί with the genitive Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων means ‘above’ the Danaans (cf. the stock epithet in 232). ἠμὲν … ἠδ’ … ἠδ’ ‘both … and … and’ lists three occasions: war (πτολέμῳ, a by-form of πολέμῳ), ‘any other work’, and the feast (δαίθ’ is δαιτί, elided). γερούσιον ‘of the elders’ and αἴθοπα ‘fire-faced’ both go with οἶνον; κέρωνται is the middle subjunctive of κεράννυμι ‘mix’ after ὅτε πέρ τε.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γάρ τ’ ἄλλοι γε κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
δαιτρὸν πίνωσιν, σὸν δὲ πλεῖον δέπας αἰεὶ
ἕστηχ’, ὥς περ ἐμοί, πιέειν ὅτε θυμὸς ἀνώγοι.
sentences.l:
For even if the other long-haired-of-head Achaeans
drink their allotted portion, yet your cup, full, always
stands, as for me, to drink whenever the heart bids.
sentences.i: For even if the other long-haired Achaeans drink their allotted portion, your cup stands always full, as mine does, for you to drink whenever your heart bids.
sentences.n: εἴ περ … ‘even if’ grants a point before the contrast σὸν δέ ‘but yours’. δαιτρὸν πίνωσιν ‘drink their allotted portion’ is the usual explanation of δαιτρόν, a rare word. πλεῖον ‘full’ and αἰεί ‘always’ go with δέπας ‘cup’, and ἕστηχ’ is ἕστηκε, the perfect of ἵστημι ‘stands’, with κ made χ before the rough breathing of ὥς. ὥς περ ἐμοί ‘just as for me’; πιέειν is the epic infinitive of πίνω’s aorist stem, and ὅτε θυμὸς ἀνώγοι ‘whenever the heart bids’ is a general clause (ἀνώγοι is the optative of ἄνωγα). κάρη κομόωντες ‘long-haired’ is the stock epithet of the Achaeans.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὄρσευ πόλεμον δ’ οἷος πάρος εὔχεαι εἶναι.
sentences.l: But rouse yourself to war, such as you formerly boast to be.”
sentences.i: But rouse yourself for war, and be the man you have always boasted that you are.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ‘but’ turns from praise to a demand. ὄρσευ is ὄρσεο, the aorist imperative middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’ (the same verb as ὄρσ’ in 204). πόλεμον δ’ is πόλεμόνδε ‘to war’, with the suffix -δε of direction. οἷος πάρος εὔχεαι εἶναι is ‘such as you boast to be, as before’: εὔχεαι is the epic second person of εὔχομαι, which with an infinitive means ‘claim, boast’, not ‘pray’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἰδομενεὺς Κρητῶν ἀγὸς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The reply formula: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ ‘and him in turn’, with τόν the old pronoun ‘him’, Agamemnon. Ἰδομενεὺς Κρητῶν ἀγός is ‘Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans’ (ἀγός is a noun from ἄγω ‘lead’). ἀντίον ‘face to face’ is an adverb, and ηὔδα ‘spoke’ the imperfect of αὐδάω, as in προσηύδα. A new paragraph begins at 265.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη μάλα μέν τοι ἐγὼν ἐρίηρος ἑταῖρος
ἔσσομαι, ὡς τὸ πρῶτον ὑπέστην καὶ κατένευσα·
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, very much, indeed, I, a trusty companion,
will be, as at first I undertook and nodded assent;
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, I shall most surely be your trusty companion, just as I undertook at the first and nodded my assent;
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative of Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’, i.e. Agamemnon. μάλα μέν τοι ‘very much indeed’ stresses the promise (τοι is a particle here, or ‘to you’). ἐγών is the epic ἐγώ, ἐρίηρος ἑταῖρος ‘trusty companion’ a stock phrase whose first part is not fully understood, and ἔσσομαι ‘I shall be’ the epic future of εἰμί. ὡς τὸ πρῶτον ‘as at first’, ὑπέστην ‘I undertook’ (aorist of ὑφίσταμαι) and κατένευσα ‘I nodded assent’ (κατανεύω) point to an earlier promise that this part does not show.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄλλους ὄτρυνε κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιοὺς
ὄφρα τάχιστα μαχώμεθ’, ἐπεὶ σύν γ’ ὅρκι’ ἔχευαν
Τρῶες·
sentences.i: but urge on the other long-haired Achaeans, so that we may fight as quickly as possible, since the Trojans have thrown the oaths into confusion;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ‘but’ turns from Idomeneus to the army. ὄτρυνε is here an imperative of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’ (the same spelling was an imperfect in 254). ἄλλους … κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιούς is ‘the other long-haired Achaeans’; ὄφρα τάχιστα μαχώμεθ’ ‘so that as quickly as possible we may fight’ has an aorist subjunctive. σύν … ἔχευαν is tmesis: συγχέω ‘pour together’, ‘confound’, said of oaths broken; ὅρκι’ is ὅρκια ‘oaths’, elided. The colon after Τρῶες falls in the middle of line 270, so the unit ends there.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ αὖ θάνατος καὶ κήδε’ ὀπίσσω
ἔσσετ’ ἐπεὶ πρότεροι ὑπὲρ ὅρκια δηλήσαντο.
sentences.l:
and for them, in turn, death and troubles hereafter
will be, since they first did harm beyond the oaths.”
sentences.i: and death and troubles will come to them afterwards, since they were the first to do harm in breach of the oaths.”
sentences.n: τοῖσιν δ’ αὖ ‘and for them, in turn’: τοῖσιν is the old pronoun in the epic dative plural, the Trojans. θάνατος καὶ κήδε’ ‘death and troubles’ (κήδε’ is κήδεα, neuter plural of κῆδος), ὀπίσσω ‘afterwards’, ἔσσετ’ ‘will be’. ἐπεὶ πρότεροι ὑπὲρ ὅρκια δηλήσαντο is Agamemnon’s clause of 236 again, now given as Idomeneus’ reason. The speech, and the part, end here.
